title: What cache eviction policies exist (LRU, LFU, FIFO, TTL/time-based, random) and how do you choose — e.g. LRU/LFU suits a content feed (keep hot items) but is a poor fit for a session store (evicting an active session logs the user out, so size for expected sessions + use TTL) — and why does a low cache hit rate make a cache a net negative (you pay the extra network hop on every miss and still hit the DB)?
shortTitle: What cache eviction policies exist, how do you choose, and why does a low hit rate make a cache a net negative?

s1_definition.profdef: A cache has finite capacity, so when it is full it must choose a victim to remove before admitting a new entry; the rule that selects the victim is the eviction policy. Least Recently Used removes the entry untouched for the longest time, Least Frequently Used removes the entry with the fewest accesses, First In First Out removes the oldest-inserted entry regardless of use, time-to-live expiry removes entries after a fixed age, and random eviction removes an arbitrary entry. The policy must match the access pattern, because the wrong policy evicts data that is about to be needed again, collapsing the hit rate and turning the cache into pure overhead.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Rajesh keeps a small desk tray that holds only ten customer files for instant access; the rest live in the basement archive. When a new file arrives and the tray is full, he must remove one. He could remove the file he has not touched for the longest time, remove the file he has consulted the fewest times, remove whichever file arrived first, remove any file older than one hour, or just grab one at random. If he removes a file he is about to need, he makes two trips to the basement instead of one, and his tray has made him slower, not faster.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match the eviction policy to the access pattern, because a cache with a low hit rate costs you a network hop on every miss and still hits the database.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A cache has finite capacity, so when it is full it must choose a victim to remove before admitting a new entry; the rule that selects the victim is the eviction policy. Least Recently Used removes the entry untouched for the longest time, Least Frequently Used removes the entry with the fewest accesses, First In First Out removes the oldest-inserted entry regardless of use, time-to-live expiry removes entries after a fixed age, and random eviction removes an arbitrary entry. The policy must match the access pattern, because the wrong policy evicts data that is about to be needed again, collapsing the hit rate and turning the cache into pure overhead.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, Rajesh keeps a small desk tray that holds only ten customer files for instant access; the rest live in the basement archive. When a new file arrives and the tray is full, he must remove one. He could remove the file he has not touched for the longest time, remove the file he has consulted the fewest times, remove whichever file arrived first, remove any file older than one hour, or just grab one at random. If he removes a file he is about to need, he makes two trips to the basement instead of one, and his tray has made him slower, not faster.

**One line to remember:** Match the eviction policy to the access pattern, because a cache with a low hit rate costs you a network hop on every miss and still hits the database.

sections.s2_technical:
Least Recently Used tracks recency of access and evicts the entry whose last access is oldest. It fits workloads with temporal locality, where recently used items are likely to be used again soon, such as a content feed where hot articles stay hot. Caffeine implements a modern variant called Window-TinyLFU that combines recency with an admission filter: `Caffeine.newBuilder().maximumSize(10_000).build()` gives you a near-LRU cache that also resists one-hit-wonder pollution, so scanning many cold keys does not evict your genuinely hot entries.

Least Frequently Used tracks how often each entry is accessed and evicts the least-accessed entry. It fits skewed popularity where a small set of items is accessed overwhelmingly more than the rest, such as the top trading symbols. Its weakness is the aging problem: an item that was extremely popular yesterday but is dead today can keep a high count and refuse to leave, so practical LFU uses decay. You can approximate it in Caffeine via frequency-aware admission, or model it explicitly with an access counter per key.

First In First Out evicts by insertion order, ignoring usage entirely. It is cheap because it needs only a queue, but it is usually a poor cache policy because it will happily evict a hot entry simply because it was inserted early. It is acceptable only when all entries have roughly equal value and age is the only sensible dimension, such as a fixed-size buffer of recent events.

Time-to-live expiry removes an entry once it reaches a maximum age, independent of usage. This is about freshness and correctness, not capacity: a balance cached for thirty seconds guarantees the displayed figure is never more than thirty seconds stale. In Caffeine this is `expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofSeconds(30))`. TTL composes with a capacity policy — you use LRU to decide who leaves when full and TTL to decide when any entry becomes too old to trust.

Random eviction picks an arbitrary victim. It sounds naive but is surprisingly competitive under heavy skew and costs almost nothing in bookkeeping, which is why some large-scale systems use sampled random eviction (pick a few entries at random, evict the least recently used among them) as a cheap approximation of LRU.

The session store is the classic mismatch. A session is active data: evicting it under memory pressure logs a working user out mid-transaction. The correct design is not to rely on capacity eviction at all but to size the store for the expected number of concurrent sessions and let sessions leave only by TTL that matches the session timeout. Using LRU on a session store means a burst of new logins can evict the sessions of users who are actively in the middle of a transfer.

The hit-rate economics are the senior point. A cache adds a network hop. On a hit you win, because the hop to Redis is far cheaper than the database query. On a miss you lose twice: you paid the hop to Redis to discover nothing was there, and then you still paid the full database query. So the cache is only a net win when the hit rate is high enough that the wins outweigh the extra miss hops. A cache sitting at a twenty percent hit rate is actively harmful — on eighty percent of requests you have added latency and load for no benefit. The policy exists to keep the hit rate high; the wrong policy is how a cache quietly becomes a net negative.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the account-balance display service caches balances in a small in-memory cache in front of PostgreSQL.

Problem 1 — the cache is tiny and the team used First In First Out because it was simplest. Rajesh at SAV2001 is a heavily active trader whose balance is read hundreds of times an hour, but because his entry was inserted early, FIFO keeps evicting it the moment the cache fills, so his hot balance is fetched from the database again and again. This is exactly what Least Recently Used fixes: it keeps the entry that is actually being used and evicts the one nobody has touched.

Problem 2 — some balances are cached but never expire, so a balance shown on screen can be minutes stale after a transfer. This is exactly what time-to-live expiry fixes: a short TTL guarantees freshness regardless of how often the entry is read.

Problem 3 — the team also tried caching every random account id that a batch report touched once, which flooded the cache with one-hit-wonders and pushed out the genuinely hot balances, dropping the hit rate to near zero. At that point the cache was a net negative — every request paid a cache hop and still went to the database. This is exactly why the eviction policy and admission must protect hot data, and why we measure hit rate to prove the cache is earning its place.

The demo builds an LRU cache with a size limit and a TTL, loads Rajesh and Priya plus eight more accounts, drives a realistic access pattern where Rajesh is hot, and prints the hit rate under FIFO-like versus LRU behaviour so the net-negative threshold is visible.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is ten accounts, with SAV2001 (Rajesh) as the hot key read every round, and a rotating scan of eight cold accounts. The cache holds only four entries with a thirty-second TTL.

Step 1: The first read of SAV2001 misses the cache, so the service reads PostgreSQL, gets one million rupees, and stores it. The miss counter is one.

Step 2: Each round also reads one cold account from the rotating scan. Because the cache holds only four entries and the scan touches eight different keys, the cold keys constantly evict each other.

Step 3: Because the cache uses access-order LRU, every read of SAV2001 moves it to the most-recently-used position, so it survives eviction even though cold keys keep churning. Under a FIFO policy SAV2001 would have been evicted by insertion age, and every round would miss on the hot key too.

Step 4: Over fifty rounds the hot key is served from cache on all but the first read, while the cold scan misses almost every time because the working set exceeds capacity.

Step 5: The service reports the hit rate. The hot key contributes many hits, but the cold scan contributes many misses, so the overall rate reflects the mismatch between working-set size and cache size. The demo warns when the rate falls below fifty percent, the point where the extra cache hop on misses starts to outweigh the savings.

```
2026-10-24 18:05:01 [INFO] Hot key SAV2001 served; cache size=4
2026-10-24 18:05:01 [INFO] Hit rate=50.0% misses=50 (DB hops)
2026-10-24 18:05:01 [WARNING] Hit rate below 50% — cache may be a NET NEGATIVE here
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Request: getBalance("SAV2001")  (HOT)        Request: getBalance("ACC3") (COLD scan)
    │                                            │
    ▼                                            ▼
  LruTtlCache.get                              LruTtlCache.get
    │ hit (moved to MRU) ✓                       │ miss (evicted by churn) ✗
    ▼                                            ▼
  return 1,000,000  (no DB hop)                AccountRepository.findById → DB (2ms hop)
    │                                            │ put(ACC3) → may evict least-recently-used
    │                                            ▼
    │                                          return balance
    ▼                                            ▼
  hits++                                       misses++  (paid hop + DB)
    │                                            │
    └───────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                    ▼
            hitRate = hits / (hits + misses)
            if < 50%  →  cache is a NET NEGATIVE
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A cache has finite capacity, so when it fills up it must pick an entry to evict, and the rule that picks the victim is the eviction policy. The main policies are Least Recently Used, which removes the entry nobody has touched for the longest time, Least Frequently Used, which removes the entry accessed the fewest times, First In First Out, which removes the oldest-inserted entry regardless of use, time-to-live expiry, which removes entries once they pass a maximum age, and random, which removes an arbitrary entry. The policy is not a detail — it decides what stays hot, and the wrong policy quietly evicts the data you are about to need.

The way I choose is to match the policy to the access pattern. For a content feed or a hot-balance lookup, where recently or frequently used items are likely to be used again, Least Recently Used or Least Frequently Used is right because it keeps the hot set resident. For data where freshness matters, such as a displayed balance, I add a short time-to-live so the figure is never more than a few seconds stale, and I treat that as composing on top of the capacity policy rather than replacing it. First In First Out I avoid as a primary cache policy because it will evict a hot entry simply for being old, and random I reserve for the cheap sampled approximations that large systems use when bookkeeping cost matters.

The session store is the example I always give for a mismatch. A session is active data, so evicting it under memory pressure logs a working user out in the middle of a transfer. The fix is not to tune the eviction policy but to stop relying on capacity eviction at all: I size the store for the expected number of concurrent sessions and let entries leave only by a time-to-live that matches the session timeout, so a burst of new logins can never evict someone who is mid-transaction.

The economics are the point I close on, because this is where engineers get burned. A cache adds a network hop. On a hit you win, because the hop to Redis is far cheaper than the database query. On a miss you lose twice — you paid the hop to Redis to find nothing, and then you still paid the full database query. So a cache only earns its place when the hit rate is high enough that the wins outweigh the extra miss cost. A cache sitting at twenty percent hit rate is actively harmful: on eighty percent of requests you have added latency and load for zero benefit.

In my banking work I caught exactly this. A balance cache was being polluted by a batch report that scanned thousands of distinct account ids once each, flooding out the genuinely hot balances and dropping the hit rate to near zero, at which point the cache was pure overhead. We fixed it by using a recency-and-frequency-aware policy with an admission filter so one-hit-wonders could not evict hot entries, by keeping the cache sized to the real working set, and crucially by putting a Prometheus gauge on the hit rate with an alert that fires if it falls below fifty percent, because that threshold is the line where a cache stops helping and starts hurting.
